newsitem.title: USA: Hot toys gone in a puff from retailer shelves.
newsitem.headline: Hot toys gone in a puff from retailer shelves.

text.p: A plush red doll with a great sense of humour, a plastic box that's useless without a television set and a blond who has yet to lose any of her mass appeal are topping Christmas wish lists, toy retailers said.
Tickle Me Elmo, Nintendo 64 and various versions of Barbie are flying off store shelves nationwide in the first week of the official holiday shopping season.
"Tickle Me Elmo's success caught us completely off guard," said Joe Young, inventory control manager at Toys R Us Inc.'s Midwest regional headquarters in Joliet, Ill.
The doll, one of eight types of Elmos manufactured by Tyco Preschool, giggles, then heaves with laughter, as its tummy is tickled.

"We always felt the item was a good item," said Neil Friedman, president of Tyco Preschool, a unit of Tyco Toys Inc. "But it's turned into a phenomenon, and that's the kind of thing you can't project."
The $28 doll is so hot the company will not be able to meet demand for Christmas, said Friedman.
But frantic Santas will continue to scramble to find one of the hottest toys in years: Nintendo 64.

"I wish I had a truckload of them right now," said Don Worley, manager of a Kmart Inc. store in Los Angeles. "It only took about two minutes to sell out of our first shipment three weeks ago. We're expecting more, but they're being allocated by the manufacturer."
Some retailers are calling Nintendo 64 the hottest Christmas toy in more than 15 years.

"One of the managers likened it to the Cabbage Patch phenomenon of the early 1980s," said Toys R Us' Young. "But that was just a $39 toy compared to $200 for the Nintendo 64. Obviously customers are willing to pay the price."

"If you haven't seen it, you wouldn't get it (understand why it such a hot commodity)," explained Dan Provost, Northeast inventory control manager for Toys R Us. "But if you've seen it, you would understand."
Among the lucky consumers who "got" Nintendo was Bonnie Nadeau, a grandmother of six who was able to pick up one of the last Nintendo 64 units at a Toys R Us store in Milwaukee.
"I was just at the right place at the right time," she said.

Nadeau wound up paying a total of $320 for the game unit and three extra controllers for multi-player gaming. She also expressed surprise that new game cartridges are expected to cost more than $85 each when they become available.

A random sampling of toy retailers from Boston to Florida to California indicates that Nintendo 64 alone could fuel a projected 3 percent to 4 percent increase in overall toy sales in 1996 to more than $20 billion. The Toy Manufacturers Association, an industry trade group, also projected that overall toy and game sales will top $21 billion in 1997.

"Nintendo 64 is one of the hottest toys we're selling right now," said a manager of a Wal-Mart Stores Inc. unit in Florida who asked not to be identified. "Fortunately, we have enough so far to meet demand."

But the champ in terms of sales consistency is still holding her own in 1996. Various types of Mattel's Barbie continue to find their way into shopping carts, 37 years after the curvy doll's introduction.
"Holiday Barbie was a hot item ever since it became available in October," said the Florida Wal-Mart manager.
Mattel sold $1.4 billion worth of Barbie dolls, accessories and related merchandise in 1995, according to company spokeswoman Sara Rozales.
"Little girls just like to play with this doll," explained Rozales. "And adult collectors are big fans as well."
With more than 100 different types of Barbie dolls created each year, "there's a Barbie that appeals to everyone," said Rozales.
Tickle Me Elmo, Nintendo 64 and Barbie are not the only toys this holiday season that kids are asking for.

Other popular toys this season include merchandise linked to the films "101 Dalmatians," "Space Jam" and "Toy Story," which was released in theatres in time for the Christmas 1995 season. Perennial favourites like Monopoly, Tonka trucks and Lego blocks also continue to attract buyers, retailers said.
But parents are being warned that demand for the hottest toys probably won't die down before Dec. 25, making it that much more imperative that alternatives are selected.
As Toys R Us' Jones notes, "even my own daughter wants a Tickle Me Elmo doll. We should have more in this week."
